en: Thus have I heard: The Discourse on the Great Exposition of Kamma (Mahākammavibhaṅgasutta), Majjhima Nikāya 136. Thus have I heard: [One time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you about the exposition of kamma. Listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) Here, bhikkhus, some person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. He experiences the result of that kamma in two ways: either in this very life or in the next existence. (2) Then, bhikkhus, some other person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. He does not experience the result of that kamma in this very life, but he experiences it in the next existence.

(3) Then, bhikkhus, some other person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. He does not experience the result of that kamma in this very life, nor does he experience it in the next existence; rather, that kamma remains stored up. (4) Then, bhikkhus, some other person does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. He experiences the result of that kamma in two ways: either in this very life or in the next existence. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Blessed One then spoke further: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) Here, bhikkhus, some person performs wholesome deeds with a mind full of lust, hatred, and delusion. He experiences the result of that kamma in two ways: either in this very life or in the next existence. (2) Then, bhikkhus, some other person performs wholesome deeds with a mind full of lust, hatred, and delusion. He does not experience the result of that kamma in this very life, but he experiences it in the next existence. (3) Then, bhikkhus, some other person performs wholesome deeds with a mind full of lust, hatred, and delusion. He does not experience the result of that kamma in this very life, nor does he experience it in the next existence; rather, that kamma remains stored up. (4) Then, bhikkhus, some other person performs wholesome deeds with a mind free from lust, hatred, and delusion. He experiences the result of that kamma in two ways: either in this very life or in the next existence. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Blessed One then spoke further: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) Here, bhikkhus, some person performs unwholesome deeds with a mind full of lust, hatred, and delusion. He experiences the result of that kamma in two ways: either in this very life or in the next existence. (2) Then, bhikkhus, some other person performs unwholesome deeds with a mind full of lust, hatred, and delusion. He does not experience the result of that kamma in this very life, but he experiences it in the next existence. He does not experience the result of that kamma in this very life, nor does he experience it in the next existence; rather, that kamma remains stored up. He experiences the result of that kamma in two ways: either in this very life or in the next existence. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time the Venerable Samiddhi was dwelling in a forest hut.
Then the wanderer Potaliputta, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the Venerable Samiddhi; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Samiddhi.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Potaliputta said this to the Venerable Samiddhi:
"Friend Samiddhi, I have heard this directly from the ascetic Gotama, and I have received it directly from him:
'Bodily action is futile, verbal action is futile; only mental action is real.'"
“Is there such an attainment, having entered which one feels nothing at all?
“Do not say so, friend Potaliputta! Do not say so, friend Potaliputta! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. For the Blessed One would not speak thus:
‘Bodily action is vain, verbal action is vain; only mental action is real.’”
“There is indeed, friend, that attainment, having entered which one does not experience anything at all.
“How long has it been since you went forth, friend Samiddhi?
“Not long, friend; three years.”
“What shall we now say to the elder bhikkhus here, when even a bhikkhu so newly ordained as this thinks that the Teacher must be protected?
Friend Samiddhi, having performed an intentional deed by body, speech, or mind, what does one experience?
“Friend Potaliputta, having performed an intentional deed by body, speech, or mind, one experiences suffering.”
Then the wanderer Potaliputta neither approved nor rejected the words of the Venerable Samiddhi;
without approving or rejecting them, he rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after the wanderer Potaliputta had left, the Venerable Samiddhi approached the Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the Venerable Samiddhi reported to the Venerable Ānanda everything that had been said in his conversation with the wanderer Potaliputta.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the Venerable Samiddhi:
“Friend Samiddhi, this is indeed a timely subject for a conversation regarding a visit to the Blessed One.
Come, friend Samiddhi, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached him, we shall report this matter to the Blessed One.
We will bear it in mind exactly as the Blessed One explains it to us.”
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Samiddhi replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Samiddhi approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Samiddhi and the wanderer Potaliputta.
When this was said, the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, I do not even recall ever having seen the wanderer Potaliputta, much less having such a conversation with him.
And yet, Ānanda, this misguided man Samiddhi has given a categorical answer to a question that required an analytical response.”
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
“But, Bhante, if what the Venerable Samiddhi spoke was intended thus:
‘Whatever is felt, that is suffering’?”
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Do you see, Ānanda, the mental wandering of this foolish man Udāyī?
I already knew it, Ānanda.”
‘Just now, as this foolish man Udāyin is emerging, he will emerge improperly.
Ānanda, from the very beginning, the wanderer Potaliputta asked about the three kinds of feeling.
If, Ānanda, this foolish man Samiddhi, being thus questioned by the wanderer Potaliputta, had answered him thus:
“Having performed an intentional action, friend Potaliputta, by way of body, speech, or mind, that is to be experienced as pleasant, one experiences pleasure;
having performed an intentional action, friend Potaliputta, by way of body, speech, or mind, that is to be experienced as painful, one experiences pain;
having performed an intentional action, friend Potaliputta, by way of body, speech, or mind, that is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, one experiences neither-pain-nor-pleasure.”
"Ananda, had the foolish man Samiddhi answered thus, he would have answered Potaliputta the wanderer correctly.
But, Ananda, what do those foolish and incompetent wanderers of other sects know of the Tathagata’s Great Exposition of Kamma?
If you, Ananda, would listen as the Tathagata expounds the Great Exposition of Kamma."
“Bhagavā, this is the time;
Sugata, this is the time for the Blessed One to analyze the Great Exposition of Kamma. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Therefore, Ānanda, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Ānanda, these four types of persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four? Here, Ānanda,
a certain person here is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct,
a speaker of falsehoods, a speaker of divisive speech, a speaker of harsh speech, a speaker of idle chatter, and one who is covetous.
He is ill-willed and holds wrong view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, and engages in sexual misconduct.
He is a speaker of falsehood, a speaker of divisive speech, a speaker of harsh speech, a frivolous talker;
he is covetous, of ill will, and holds wrong view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
In this case, Ānanda, a certain person here abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech,
abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter.
He is free from covetousness, he has a mind devoid of ill will, and he holds right view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person refrains from taking life and refrains from taking what is not given in this very life.
He abstains from sexual misconduct, he abstains from false speech, he abstains from malicious speech,
he abstains from harsh speech, he abstains from idle chatter; he is free from covetousness,
he is of a mind without ill will, and he possesses right view.
Thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm,
even in hell. Here, Ānanda, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor, through striving,
through application, through diligence, and through right attention, attains such a concentration of mind that, when his mind is thus concentrated...
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees this person:

here, one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view; and with the breakup of the body, after death—
He sees one reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower world, or in hell.
He says this:
“Indeed, sirs, there are evil deeds; there is a result of misconduct.”

“I saw a person here who was a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view; after the breakup of the body, following death, I see him reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
He says this:

“It seems, sirs, that whoever is a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view, all such persons, after the breakup of the body, following death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.”
"Those who know thus know rightly; those who know otherwise, their knowledge is wrong.
Thus, whatever he has known for himself, seen for himself, and realized for himself, he adheres to that with obstinacy and attachment, and asserts it: "This alone is the truth, all else is false.
But here, Ānanda, some ascetic or brahmin, through ardor, through striving, and through application...

Through diligence and through right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees this person:

one who here has been a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view; and after the breakup of the body, after death, he sees him reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
He spoke thus:
“Indeed, sir, there are no evil deeds; there is no result of misconduct.

I saw a person here who was a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, I see him reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.”
Thus he spoke:

"Sirs, it is said that whoever kills living beings, takes what is not given, [and so on]... up to: holds wrong view, all such persons, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
Those who know this know rightly; those who know otherwise possess false knowledge."
Thus, whatever he has known for himself, seen for himself, and realized for himself, that very thing he adheres to with obstinate clinging and asserts: "This alone is the truth;

all else is false. Here, Ānanda, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor, through striving, through application, through diligence, and through right attention, attains such a concentration of mind that, when his mind is thus concentrated...
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees that person here who abstains from the destruction of life,
abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct,
abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter.
Abstaining [from these], free from covetousness, with a mind devoid of ill will, and possessing right view— after the breakup of the body, after death,
he sees that one has been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. He speaks thus:
‘Indeed, sir, there are wholesome deeds; there is a result of good conduct.

For I saw a person here who abstained from taking life, abstained from taking what is not given... [and so on] ...who held right view, and after the breakup of the body, after death, I see him reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
He speaks thus:

‘It seems, sirs, that whoever abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given... [and so on] ...up to right view, at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
Those who know thus know correctly; those who know otherwise possess false knowledge.

Thus, whatever he has known for himself, seen for himself, and realized for himself, that alone he adheres to with obstinacy and attachment, insisting upon it and declaring: ‘This alone is the truth; all else is false.’
But here, Ānanda, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through ardor, through striving,
through application, through diligence, and through right attention, attains such a concentration of mind that,
with his mind thus concentrated, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees that person here.

One who abstains from taking life ... [and so on] ... possesses right view; yet, with the breakup of the body, after death, he sees him reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower world, or in hell.
He says this:
‘Indeed, sir, there are no wholesome deeds; there is no result of good conduct.

For I saw a person here who abstained from taking life, abstained from taking what is not given... [and so on] ...who possessed right view, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, I see him reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.’”

Thus he says: “Indeed, sirs, whoever abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given... [and so on] ...and possesses right view, all such persons, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.
Those who know thus know correctly; those who know otherwise have wrong knowledge.

In this way, whatever he has known for himself, seen for himself, and realized for himself, that very thing he adheres to with obstinacy and attachment, and he declares: “This alone is the truth; anything else is false.”
In this regard, Ānanda, when a certain ascetic or brahmin says:
"Indeed, sir, there are evil deeds; there is a result of misconduct," I acknowledge this of him;
and as for what he also says:

“If he says, ‘I saw a person here who was a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view, and after the breakup of the body, after death, I see him reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell,’ I allow this of him.

But as for his saying, ‘It seems, sir, that whoever is a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view, all such persons, after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell’—this I do not allow of him.”
Furthermore, when he says:
“Those who know thus know rightly; those who know otherwise have wrong knowledge,” I do not assent to this either.

Moreover, when he dogmatically adheres to, clings to, and insists upon whatever he has personally known, personally seen, and personally realized, asserting: “Only this is true, anything else is false,” I do not assent to this either.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the great analysis of kamma is otherwise.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for that ascetic or brahmin who speaks thus:
‘There are indeed no evil deeds, there is no result of misconduct’—this I do not concede to him.
But as for what he says:

‘I have seen a person here who was a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view, and after the breakup of the body, after death, I see him reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world’—this I concede to him.
But as for what he says:

‘Indeed, sir, whoever is a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view, all such a person, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world’—I do not grant this to him;
and as for what he also says:
‘Those who know thus know rightly; those who know otherwise have wrong knowledge’—this too I do not concede to him.

And as for his insisting upon, grasping at, and adhering to whatever he has known for himself, seen for himself, and realized for himself, and declaring: ‘This alone is the truth, all else is false’—this too I do not concede to him. Why is that?
For otherwise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the great analysis of kamma is as follows:
In this regard, Ānanda, when a certain ascetic or brahmin says, ‘There indeed, sir, are wholesome kamma-formations;
there is the result of good conduct,’ I grant him this.
And when he says this:
“I saw a person here who abstained from taking life, abstained from taking what is not given... [and so on] ... possessed of right view;
with the breakup of the body, after death, I see him reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.”
I allow this of him as well;
however, as for what he says:

‘Sir, it seems that whoever abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given... [and so on] ... and possesses right view, all such persons, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world’—this I do not allow of him.
Furthermore, when he says:
“Those who know thus know rightly; those who know otherwise have wrong knowledge,” I do not concede this to him either.

Moreover, when he dogmatically adheres to, clings to, and insists upon that which he has known for himself, seen for himself, and realized for himself, asserting: “Only this is true, anything else is false,” I do not concede this to him either.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the Great Exposition of Kamma is otherwise.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for that ascetic or brahmin who speaks thus:
‘There are indeed no wholesome deeds, there is no result of good conduct’—this I do not concede to him.
But as for what he says:
‘I have seen a person here who abstained from taking life, abstained from taking what is not given... [and so forth].
‘With right view, I see that after the breakup of the body, following death, I have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell’—
this I allow of him; and as for what he says thus:
‘Sir, it is said that whoever abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given...

[and so on] ...up to right view, all such persons, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell’—this I do not concede to him.
But as for what he says: ‘Those who know thus, they know rightly’—that I do concede.”
‘Those who know otherwise have wrong knowledge’—this too I do not allow him.

And as for his adhering, grasping, and insisting with vehemence upon whatever he has known for himself, seen for himself, and understood for himself, and his declaring: ‘Only this is true, anything else is false’—this too I do not allow him. Why is that?
For otherwise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the great analysis of kamma is such:

In this case, Ānanda, there is a person who here is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...one of wrong view; with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.

Either that evil kamma to be experienced as suffering was done by him previously, or that evil kamma to be experienced as suffering was done by him later, or at the time of death he held a wrong view that was fully adopted and undertaken.

Because of that, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. However, as for his killing of living beings here, taking what is not given...

[and so on] ...up to his holding wrong view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period. In this regard, Ānanda, as for that person who here kills living beings, takes what is not given... [and so on] ...up to holding wrong view, yet with the breakup of the body after death is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world: [The Buddha continued: “Ānanda, suppose there were two brothers, both of whom were thieves. One brother would steal from time to time, while the other brother would steal frequently. Both, having been caught by the king’s men, would be brought before the king. Then the king, having had one brother executed, would banish the other brother to a frontier region. What do you think, Ānanda? Would the first brother, who stole only occasionally, be banished to the frontier region along with the second brother? “No, venerable sir. “Would the second brother, who stole frequently, be executed along with the first brother? “No, venerable sir. “In the same way, Ānanda, when a person here kills living beings, takes what is not given... [and so on] ...up to holding wrong view, yet with the breakup of the body after death is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world, it is because of the wholesome deeds they have done in the past, because of the wholesome roots they have planted in the past. But because of their killing of living beings here, taking what is not given... [and so on] ...up to their holding wrong view, they experience the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.”

Either that wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasant was performed by him previously, or that wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasant was performed by him later, or at the time of death he possessed right view that was fully undertaken and maintained.
Because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.

However, as for the fact that he here was a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given... [and so on] ...and had wrong view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.

In this regard, Ānanda, when a person here abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given... [and so on] ...up to right view, and after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world—either that wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasure was performed by him previously, or that wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasure was performed by him later, or at the time of death he possessed right view that was fulfilled and undertaken.
It is because of that that, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.

But as for that person who here abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given... and possesses right view, they experience the result of this either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.

In this regard, Ānanda, when that person who here abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given... and possesses right view, yet upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell—

Either he has previously committed that evil deed to be experienced as suffering, or he has subsequently committed that evil deed to be experienced as suffering, or at the time of death he holds a wrong view that is fully adopted and undertaken.
Because of that, with the breakup of the body after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.

"But as for that which he here refrains from taking life, refrains from taking what is not given... [and so on] ... and possesses right view: he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.

Thus, Ānanda, there is action incapable of being manifested, yet appearing capable; there is action incapable of being manifested, yet appearing incapable; there is action both capable and appearing capable; and there is action capable of being manifested, yet appearing incapable. This is what the Blessed One said.
The Venerable Ānanda, elated, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The sixth discourse, the Mahākammavibhaṅgasutta, is finished.
